clinicalPearls: Diffuse, non-scarring hair shedding that classically begins around two to three months after a triggering event such as childbirth, severe febrile illness, major surgery, crash dieting, or starting or stopping a drug

Patients often report alarming quantities of hair on the pillow, in the shower, and on the brush, yet visible baldness is unusual because shedding rarely involves more than about half of the scalp hair
The hair-pull test is positive with an increased proportion of club (telogen) hairs, and trichoscopy shows numerous empty follicles and short upright regrowing hairs
Follicular ostia are preserved, confirming a non-scarring process with excellent potential for full regrowth, which distinguishes it from cicatricial alopecias
Acute forms are self-limiting and settle within a few months once the trigger has passed, whereas chronic telogen effluvium persists beyond six months, often in middle-aged women, and fluctuates
A careful history covering events in the preceding few months, a drug review, and screening for iron deficiency, thyroid dysfunction and nutritional causes usually identifies the precipitant
Reassurance about the reversible nature is central, and treating any identified underlying cause such as iron repletion or thyroid correction is the mainstay rather than specific hair therapy
reference.pathophysiology: Telogen effluvium results from a disturbance of the normal hair cycle in which an abnormally large proportion of follicles are prematurely shifted from the growing (anagen) phase into the resting (telogen) phase. After a latency of roughly two to three months these synchronised telogen hairs are shed as new anagen hairs emerge beneath them. Recognised triggers include physiological stress such as childbirth, febrile illness and major surgery, rapid weight loss, iron and other nutritional deficiency, thyroid disturbance, and numerous drugs. Because the follicles themselves are not destroyed and the ostia remain intact, the process is non-scarring and reverses once the precipitant resolves.
additionalDifferentials: Androgenetic alopecia, which may be unmasked or accelerated by an effluvium
Alopecia areata, especially the diffuse (incognita) variant
Anagen effluvium from chemotherapy or toxin exposure
Early scarring alopecia presenting with shedding
Diffuse hair loss of systemic disease such as thyroid disorder or lupus
Nutritional or iron-deficiency related hair loss
additionalInvestigations: Hair-pull test to confirm increased telogen shedding
Trichoscopy to assess follicular ostia, hair-shaft calibre and regrowth
Full blood count and ferritin to detect iron deficiency
Targeted screening for other nutritional causes such as vitamin D or zinc where clinically indicated
Trichogram or scalp biopsy in uncertain or chronic cases to confirm the telogen ratio and exclude other diagnoses
redFlags: Loss of follicular ostia, scaling, or perifollicular erythema suggesting a scarring alopecia rather than an effluvium
Shedding that continues beyond six months or progresses despite removal of the presumed trigger
Associated systemic symptoms pointing to occult illness or malignancy
Patchy rather than diffuse loss suggesting alopecia areata or tinea capitis
reference.prognosis: Acute telogen effluvium is self-limiting and typically resolves with full regrowth over several months once the trigger has passed; chronic telogen effluvium may fluctuate over years but does not itself cause permanent baldness, although it can unmask underlying androgenetic thinning.
pitfalls: Attributing all diffuse shedding to effluvium and overlooking early androgenetic alopecia or diffuse alopecia areata
Looking back only to when shedding began rather than two to three months earlier for the true trigger
Missing a treatable systemic cause such as iron deficiency or thyroid disease
Reassuring a patient without excluding a scarring process on close scalp examination
